newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: POLICE CLAIM SERIAL KILLER INTELLIGENT
A forensic psychiatrist with the Ministry of Justice and the Health Department has warned the serial killer preying on Perth women will keep killing until caught.
The body of 27-year-old Ciara Glennon was found in bush, 40 kilometres north of Perth yesterday, three weeks after she disappeared from Claremont.
The body of Jane Rimmer, who also went missing from Claremont, was discovered in bush south of Perth last August.

Forensic psychiatrist, Anath Pullela, predicted a body would be found north of Perth, and says police should now be searching bushland to the east to find Sarah Spiers who's been missing for 15 months.
Doctor Pullela says police are looking for an intelligent killer.
ABA FINDS CANWEST IN BREACH OF FOREIGN OWNERSHIP LAWS
The Australian Broadcasting Authority believes Canadian company Canwest, which has shares in the Ten Network, is in breach of the foreign ownership laws.
The ABA has been examining recent share transactions in the Ten Group.
Section 57 of the Broadcasting Services Act provides that a foreign person must not be in a position to exercise control of a commercial television licence.
Foreign companies are allowed to be in a postion to control only 15-per cent of company interests.
The ABA says Canwest is now in a position to excercise control, and has given it six-months to rectify the situation.
A spokesman for the Federal Communications Minister, Richard Alston, says the Minister is studying the ABA report.
PSU WARNS EMPLOYMENT CONDITIONS ARE IN JEOPARDY
The Public Sector Union believes a number of employment conditions are in jeopardy as a result of Federal Government changes.
PSU Secretary Wendy Caird says changes put forward by Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith last month foreshadow the biggest battle the union has had to fight.
Mr Reith's proposals will enable individual departments to set their own pay scales, also promote the offering of individual contracts.
Ms Caird says the Government wants to take out the automatic advancement processes, conflicting with its election commitment that no worker would be worse off.
Members will be asked to vote on a proposal for a general stopwork meeting to be held on April the 24th.
QUINN PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO FRAUD

Former Coles Myer chief Brian Quinn has pleaded not guilty to conspiring with the former head of the maintenance department, Graham Lanyon, to defraud the company of more than four-million dollars to pay for his home renovations.
Giving evidence today, Mr Quinn denied he paid some of the cost of his home renovations because of a fraud squad investigation.
He told the court he did what he said he was always going to do when the work was completed on his home, and that was to pay the balance, after the company had contributed an amount.
WOMAN REFUSES TO COLLECT SON'S BODY
The mother of a man shot by police during a drug raid in Newcastle last year, says a coronial inquest held last month has failed to reveal all the facts behind the shooting.
Muswellbrook woman Robyn Green has refused a request from the coroner to collect her son's body from the morgue for burial, saying she wants an independant inquiry into the shooting.
The coroner last month found police shot Paul Green in self-defence, after he pointed a loaded shotgun at them.
But, Robyn Green says she wants the body kept at the morgue, so further medical evidence can be taken, if the family suceeds in forcing a wide-ranging inquiry into the shooting.
CLAIMS MONEY DOESN'T REACH ABORIGINAL COMMUNITIES

A member of the National Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation says some Aborigines are living in conditions worse than many third world countries because government bureaucrats are milking the coffers.
Jackie Huggins says many Aboriginal communities don't have adequate housing, clean water or sewerage.
She says it's difficult for Aborigines to break the poverty cycle and improve their lifestyle when almost 70 per cent of government funding doesn't reach them.
RAFTER WINS FIRST RUBBER
Australia's Patrick Rafter has given the home side a one-nil lead in the Davis Cup quarter final against the Czech Republic at Adelaide's Memorial Drive.
After racing to a two set lead at 6-1, 7-6, the Queenslander lost the next set 6-4 to Martin Damm.
However the 43-world-ranked player took the fourth set 6-4. Rafter says despite losing the third set, he was pleased to get in the big shots when it counted.
CHIEF JUSTICE BACKS COMMISSIONER FOR CHILDREN
The Chief Justice of the Family Court says the rights and interests of children should be one area which spans idealogical divides.
Justice Alistair Nicholson is backing the introduction of a National Commissioner for Children in conjunction with the UN convention on the rights of children.

He says the role of a National Commissioner should have statutary independence, by reporting to parliament rather than a minister, should be accessible to all, and be close to decision-making bodies concerned with children.
Justice Nicholson told a conference on children's rights in Brisbane, it's absurd that Australia's elected representatives are unable to match the bulk of the international community.
